# Chapter Fifteen: Clash of Titans & The Shared Scream

> *"You cannot break someone who has already pieced themselves back together in the dark."*

The observation bridge of *The Black Leviathan* was a cathedral of black chrome and panoramic viewports overlooking the burning wreckage of New Tortuga.

Standing in the center of the chamber was Baron Marcus Vargas. 

He was no longer wearing his aristocratic robes. He stood encased in a massive, hydraulically reinforced powered exoskeleton, twin high-caliber rotary blasters mounted to his forearms and energy blades humming along his wrists.

“You are remarkably persistent, Campbell,” Vargas chuckled, turning to face them. “Just like your father. But this is where the legend ends.”

Before Kael could raise his rifle, Vargas’s exoskeleton surged forward with impossible speed. A backhand blow from the armored brute caught Kael squarely in the chest, shattering his rifle and launching the engineer across the bridge into a steel bulkhead, knocking him senseless.

“Kael!” Gracie cried out, drawing her pistols.

Vargas didn't shoot. Instead, he tapped a control on his gauntlet.

A high-frequency sonic pulse erupted from the ceiling emitters—a specialized neural scrambler tuned to illicit military cyberware.

The frequency hit the Box in Gracie’s neck like a bolt of lightning.

Agony—pure, unadulterated, hundred-year-old torture—exploded through Gracie’s central nervous system. Her pistols slipped from her numb fingers, clattering across the deck. She fell to her knees, vomiting blood as her vision flashed blinding white and screaming scarlet.

*THE FIRE!* the passenger wailed, thrashing in the depths of her mind. *HE HAS THE KEY! HE'S PEELING OUR BRAIN APART! GRACIE! HELP US!*

Vargas stepped forward, his heavy armored boot planting itself firmly on Gracie’s chest, pinning her to the floor. He drew an obsidian extraction needle from his hip, its tip humming with harvesting energy.

“Vengeance was an artist,” Vargas purred, pressing the needle against the raw scar at the base of her skull. “He spent a century breaking this mind, and now it belongs to me. You were never a warrior, little girl. You were just the delivery truck.”

Gracie stared up into Vargas’s cold, arrogant eyes.

Through the blinding agony, through the screams of the hundred-year-old ghost, a cold, crystal-clear realization took hold.

She had spent three months fighting the Box. She had spent three months trying to silence the ghost, treating it like a curse, running from the pain.

*Stop fighting it,* she thought into the dark.

*What?* the passenger gasped, weeping in agony.

*Stop running from the pain,* Gracie spoke to the ghost with every ounce of soul she possessed. *He wants to hear us scream? Let’s give him what he wants. Together.*

In that instant, the barrier between Gracie Campbell and the century-tortured prisoner dissolved. 

Gracie stopped resisting the neural feedback. She opened her mind, embracing the totality of the hundred years of torment, the fire, the needles, the rage of a soul that had survived a century of hell and the fury of a girl who had dragged herself through a garbage chute to be free.

She synchronized her neural accelerator directly with the Box’s quantum frequency.

Gracie looked up at Vargas, and through the blood on her teeth, she smiled.

Then she screamed.

It was not a scream of defeat. It was a weapon.

A blinding, sapphire shockwave of raw quantum energy and hundred-year-old neural agony erupted from Gracie’s body. The concussive blast shattered the ceiling scramblers, blew the observation windows into spiderwebs of fracture, and threw Vargas’s massive exoskeleton backward ten feet.

Before Vargas could recover, Gracie blurred forward.

Her cybernetic reflexes were faster than lightning. She grabbed Vargas’s armored wrist, drove her palm into his chest plate, and channeled the entire stored reserve of the Box’s neural torment directly into his exoskeleton’s cybernetic uplink.

A blinding arc of blue electricity surged into Vargas’s nervous system.

The warlord shrieked as a century of distilled phantom torture flooded his brain. His eyes bulged, his cybernetic implants sparked and smoked, and with a sickening pop of overloaded electronics, his exoskeleton locked up and collapsed to the deck like a pile of scrap iron.

Vargas lay twitching, completely catatonic, his mind shattered by the very weapon he had sought to claim.

Gracie stood over him, chest heaving, blood dripping from her brow. 

In her head, the Box was quiet. For the first time, the passenger was laughing—a quiet, breathless, victorious laugh that echoed with deep, profound peace.

“We won,” Gracie whispered aloud.

*We won,* the ghost replied.
